paragraphs.heading: Swirls in the ocean
paragraphs.text: An eddy is a movement of fluid that departs from the fluid's general flow. Eddies are common in the ocean, and they range from centimetres to hundreds of kilometres across. The smallest may last only seconds, while the larger ones may persist for months to years. Oceanographers call an eddy a mesoscale eddy when it is between about 10 and 500 km in diameter and lasts for days to months.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds
paragraphs.text: Mesoscale eddies fall into two categories. Static eddies are caused by flow around an obstacle. Transient eddies are caused by what is called baroclinic instability. A gradient in sea surface height gives rise to a jet or current, and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current is one. As part of a baroclinically unstable system, the current meanders and creates eddies, much as a meandering river forms an oxbow lake. Eddies of this type have been observed in many major currents, including the Gulf Stream, the Agulhas Current and the Kuroshio Current.

paragraphs.heading: Inside an eddy
paragraphs.text: The currents of a mesoscale eddy flow in a roughly circular path around its centre. They may rotate in either of two senses, cyclonic or anticyclonic. The water in an eddy is usually a different water mass from the water outside, with a different temperature and salinity. These properties are linked directly to the rotation. Warm eddies rotate anticyclonically, and cold eddies rotate cyclonically.

paragraphs.heading: Moving heat
paragraphs.text: Mesoscale eddies play a crucial part in moving heat toward the poles and in maintaining heat gradients at different depths. As they move they carry unusually warm or cold water, so in certain parts of the ocean they have an important influence on how heat is transported. Their circulation may be vigorous, which makes them a concern for naval and commercial operations at sea.

paragraphs.heading: Carrying life and litter
paragraphs.text: Ocean and atmospheric currents move particles, debris and organisms across the globe. Moving organisms such as phytoplankton is essential for preserving ecosystems, but oil and other pollutants get mixed into the flow too and can be carried far from where they started. Eddy formations circulate trash and other pollutants, gathering them into concentrated areas. Researchers are tracking these areas to improve clean-up and pollution prevention. The spread and motion of plastics caused by eddies in natural water bodies can be predicted with Lagrangian transport models.
